title: Panic attack: what to do
def: A panic attack is a sudden wave of fear with a racing heart, fast breathing, shaking, or a sense of doom; it peaks within minutes and passes.
look: fast breathing, tingling hands, chest tightness
a strong urge to flee
symptoms that ease within about 20 minutes
use: Sit down, breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in, name five things you can see, and remind yourself it will pass. Stay with someone who is panicking and speak calmly.
not: Do not assume chest pain is panic if the person has heart risks, is older, or the pain spreads to the arm or jaw; treat it as a medical emergency.
steps: Sit or stand still somewhere steady.
Breathe in for 4, out for 6, for a few minutes.
Name what you see, hear, and feel.
call: Call 911 for chest pain, fainting, or trouble breathing that does not ease. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Scared or lost: calming down so you can act
also: I think we are lost and I'm scared
def: Fear in a bad situation is normal; slowing your breathing and taking one small practical step at a time brings back clear thinking.
look: racing thoughts and an urge to hurry
a group arguing or splitting up
darkness or weather adding pressure
use: Stop, sit, breathe slowly, then do the next useful thing: check water, warmth, and shelter, look at the map, and decide together.
not: Do not rush off, split up, or make big decisions in the first minutes of fear.
call: Call 911 if you have signal and are lost or hurt.

title: Thoughts of suicide or not wanting to be here
also: I don't want to be here
def: Thoughts of suicide or of not wanting to be alive are a sign of serious pain and deserve immediate support, not judgment.
look: talk of being a burden or wanting to die
giving things away or saying goodbye
access to a gun, pills, or other means
use: Take it seriously, stay with the person if it is safe, ask directly whether they are thinking of suicide, listen, and help them call or text 988. Move guns and pills away if you safely can.
not: Do not leave a person at risk alone, promise to keep it secret, or argue about whether they really mean it.
call: Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Shaken after a close call, crash, or bad hunt
def: After a frightening event it is common to feel shaky, numb, jumpy, or replay it for days; for most people these reactions fade over a few weeks.
look: trouble sleeping and replaying the event
feeling on edge or numb
avoiding the place or activity
use: Get safe, warm, and fed, talk with someone you trust, keep simple routines, and give it time.
not: Do not use alcohol or drugs to blot it out, and do not push yourself to retell every detail if you do not want to.
call: Seek help if reactions last more than a few weeks or interfere with daily life. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Grief after a death, and grief after a kill
def: Grief is the natural response to loss; it can come in waves of sadness, anger, guilt, or numbness, and some hunters feel a quieter grief after a kill.
look: waves of feeling that come and go
tiredness and poor sleep
guilt or replaying what happened
use: Let the feelings come, talk with people who care, keep basic routines, and honor the loss in your own way.
not: Do not judge yourself for how you grieve or how long it takes.
call: Reach out to a clinician if grief stays crushing for months or you have thoughts of harming yourself. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: When to get professional mental health help
def: Professional help makes sense when distress lasts for weeks, gets in the way of work, sleep, or family, or includes thoughts of self-harm.
look: low mood or worry most days for two weeks or more
drinking or drug use to cope
thoughts of death or self-harm
use: Talk to a doctor or a licensed counselor; the 988 Lifeline is free, confidential, and available 24/7 by call or text.
not: Do not wait for it to get worse before reaching out.
call: Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Exhaustion, poor sleep, and bad decisions in the field
def: Fatigue, cold, hunger, and poor sleep slow thinking and make people take risks they would never take rested.
look: clumsiness and short temper
pushing on to reach a goal despite warning signs
forgetting simple steps
use: Stop, eat, drink, warm up, and rest before any big decision; set a turnaround time and keep it.
not: Do not drive, climb, or handle firearms when you are exhausted.

title: Alcohol and drugs as a way to cope outdoors
def: Alcohol and drugs can feel like relief, but outdoors they raise the risk of hypothermia, falls, drowning, and firearm accidents, and they deepen low mood afterward.
look: drinking to sleep or calm down
drinking around water, fire, or firearms
needing more to get the same effect
use: Keep alcohol away from firearms, boats, and climbing, and look for other ways to unwind: food, warmth, talk, and rest.
not: Do not mix alcohol with firearms, driving, or cold-weather travel.
call: SAMHSA's National Helpline, 1-800-662-4357, is free and confidential. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Helping a friend in crisis
def: Helping a friend in crisis mostly means staying with them, listening without fixing, and connecting them with help.
look: a friend withdrawing or talking about hopelessness
sudden changes in behavior
talk of suicide
use: Ask how they are and listen, say you care, ask directly about suicide if you are worried, and help them call or text 988 or a professional.
not: Do not lecture, minimize their feelings, or take over their choices.
call: Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
